items.title: CBRE, North America Data Center Trends H1 2026
items.detail: 7,481 MW under construction across the eight US primary markets, up 24.8%. Vacancy 1.4%, net absorption 1,456 MW, over 80% of construction preleased.
items.effect: Hillsboro / Portland updated 430 to 491 MW, same source, newer vintage. The other seven markets keep their Knight Frank figures: CBRE counts primary-market colocation inventory, Knight Frank counts every operator's live IT capacity, so the gap is a population difference, not a discrepancy.

items.title: TCS / HyperVault, up to 1 GW in Telangana
items.detail: Up to Rs 70,000 crore, roughly $8.4bn, on 264 acres near Hyderabad, built in phases against customer demand. No completion date given.
items.effect: No change to today's figures. Announced capacity with no energization date is a claim, not load.

items.title: Vantage, Project Latigo, Laramie County, Wyoming
items.detail: Zone change approved unanimously. 480 MW across 1,835 acres, up to $20bn, with onsite generation, 12 miles south of Cheyenne.
items.effect: Not added. The campus layer comes from Epoch AI's dataset; a site enters when Epoch picks it up, because mixing news-sourced sites into a single-source layer breaks its provenance. A zoning approval is also permission, not load.

items.title: Epoch AI revises two campuses down
items.detail: Google New Albany cut from 453 to 333 MW and Meta Aiken from 142 to 69 MW in Epoch's frontier data centre dataset. Same source, newer estimate, no change of method.
items.effect: Mapped campus capacity 13,257 to 13,064 MW, down 193 MW, almost all of it US. Country and metro layers are unaffected: both sites sit outside a mapped metro, so nothing was double counted either way.

items.title: IEA publishes 485 TWh for 2025
items.detail: Key Questions on Energy and AI (16 April 2026) puts global data centre electricity at 485 TWh in 2025, up 17% on the year. The page is anchored to the IEA's 415 TWh for 2024, from Energy and AI.
items.effect: Not adopted, and the anchor is unchanged. The whole capacity basis here is IEA installed capacity for 2024 (122.2 GW); dividing 2025 energy by 2024 capacity would move kIea from 0.398 to 0.453 on a year mismatch rather than on evidence. It becomes adoptable when the IEA publishes a 2025 capacity figure to pair it with. Recorded in policy.json.

items.title: Oregon puts data centres in their own rate class
items.detail: The POWER Act (House Bill 3546, 2025) requires Oregon utilities to serve large energy use facilities of 20 MW and above under a separate schedule on contracts of ten years or longer. The PUC approved Portland General Electric's version in Order No. 26-239 on 10 July 2026, raising data centre rates about 29% on average while every other class fell. Pacific Power's is pending in Docket UE 463.
items.effect: No figure moved. Added to the regulatory set, where it attaches to Hillsboro / Portland — whose 491 MW (CBRE, H1 2026) is unchanged. Cost allocation is not generation, so no capacity or consumption value depends on it.

items.title: Pennsylvania sets a model large-load tariff
items.detail: PUC Final Order of 13 May 2026, Docket M-2025-3054271, adopted at the 30 April public meeting. It covers customers above 50 MW individually or 100 MW in aggregate: cost causation for interconnection, deposits and collateral against stranded cost, six-month study timelines, minimum contract terms and exit provisions, a public interconnection queue.
items.effect: No figure moved. Added to the regulatory set as a national-thread item; Pennsylvania has no mapped metro on this page, so nothing attaches to a marker. Found on a gap check rather than published this fortnight — it is here because the set had Ohio and Oregon but not the one statewide model tariff written for the same problem.

items.title: China's energy regulator: internet data services power use up 44%
items.detail: At its Jul 30, 2026 press conference the National Energy Administration reported that electricity used by the internet data services industry reached 49.4 billion kWh (49.4 TWh) in the first half of 2026, up 44% year on year. It is an official, measured series, but it counts consumption by enterprises classified as internet data services, a narrower and differently drawn population than the 260 TWh (2024) figure this page uses for China. Separately, a Wood Mackenzie projection of 774 TWh by 2030 (reported by China Daily, Sep 3, 2026) is a consultancy forecast and does not qualify under Test 1.
items.effect: No figure moved. China stays on 260 TWh (2024), scope mismatch declared. The NEA value is a half-year, 2026-vintage, industry-classified total, so it cannot be set against 2024 capacity, and it does not say whether telecom and 5G network rooms are in or out, which is the question that would settle China. Watching for a full-year NEA or CEC value.
items.src: National Energy Administration (China), press conference transcript, Jul 30, 2026

items.title: Pennsylvania opens a second data center proceeding
items.detail: At its Sep 10, 2026 public meeting the Pennsylvania PUC voted 5-0 to have staff propose updates to its emergency curtailment rules and hold a technical conference on cost allocation for data centers, with a tentative order due at the Oct 1, 2026 meeting and a final vote targeted for Jan 28, 2027. A companion motion set up a ratemaking working group (Docket M-2026-3064953). This follows the model large-load tariff (Docket M-2025-3054271) already in the regulatory set.
items.effect: No figure moved. Curtailment and cost allocation are not generation, and Pennsylvania has no mapped metro, so nothing attaches to a marker. The existing Pennsylvania entry is left as is until the tentative order is published with a docket number.

items.title: Eurostat publishes a measured data center electricity series
items.detail: Dataset isoc_env_ict_nrg, "Data centres' electricity consumption", last updated Jul 27, 2026, covering 2020-2024 in terajoules for 42 countries. The EU energy statistics regulation obliges member states to file data center energy use above 1 MW with Eurostat annually, colocation and enterprise alike, so this is measured national reporting rather than a consultancy model.
items.effect: No figure moved. The series reproduces three of the five anchors for 2024 within about 1% - Ireland 6.969 TWh against the CSO's 6.973, the Netherlands 5.093 against the CBS's 5.100, France 4.348 against SDES's 4.3 - which is independent corroboration of the metro basis rather than a new input. Germany is the live question and is recorded in policy.json: the series passes Test 1 there but fails Test 2 at 1.90. Finland, Poland and Spain would pass both tests, but admitting anchors moves kNat and needs calib.json, which this path will not carry.

items.title: Imperial Irrigation District adopts a curtail-first large load tariff
items.detail: The IID board voted unanimously on Sep 16, 2026 to adopt a Large Load Tariff for customers above 20 MW: infrastructure cost recovery, a minimum monthly charge of at least 85% of contracted energy, a fifteen-year commitment, cash deposits, and first place in line to be shut off when demand peaks.
items.effect: No figure moved, and it is not in the regulatory set. The tariff document on iid.com refused the request from here, so only the press account could be read, and that set holds filings read on the filing itself. Imperial Valley has no mapped metro, so nothing would attach to a marker either way. Recorded here so a later run can promote it once the document is reachable.

items.title: China Electricity Council: internet data services power use past 60 TWh this year
items.detail: At the 2026 Energy Green Development Conference, reported by CCTV News on Sep 16, 2026, the China Electricity Council said national electricity use by the internet data services industry has passed 60 billion kWh (60 TWh) so far in 2026, up more than 40% year on year and already far above the full-year 2024 level. It described the first half, the 49.4 TWh the National Energy Administration reported in July, as already close to that full-year 2024 total. The council's Pan Yuelong separately projected national computing-power electricity reaching 800 TWh by 2030, about 6% of all electricity used in China.
items.effect: No figure moved. China stays on 260 TWh (2024), scope mismatch declared. This is the same narrow industry classification as the National Energy Administration's half-year figure, it is a partial year, and it is 2026 vintage, so it cannot be set against 2024 capacity and Test 2 cannot be run on it at all. It does sharpen the mismatch rather than settle it: the council puts the full-year 2024 total for that classification close to 49.4 TWh, roughly a fifth of the 260 TWh this page uses for China in the same year, which is direct evidence the two sources count different populations. It still does not say whether telecom and 5G network rooms are inside the wider figure, which is the question that would settle China. The 800 TWh 2030 number is a projection and fails Test 1. The council's own site timed out from here, so this rests on the CCTV News account as carried by 21st Century Business Herald.
items.src: China Electricity Council, via CCTV News, Sep 16, 2026

items.title: Pennsylvania conditions data center permits on local approval
items.detail: Executive Order 2026-05, signed Aug 18, 2026, directs the Department of Environmental Protection to review a data center permit application only where the developer has made a legally binding commitment, through a Consent Order and Agreement, to the Governor's Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) requirements covering energy affordability, environmental protection, workforce and economic development, transparency and community engagement, and has already secured every required local approval. It removes all AI data center projects from the state's Permit Fast Track program and bars nondisclosure agreements on data center projects.
items.effect: No figure moved. Permitting conditions are not generation, and Pennsylvania has no mapped metro on this page, so nothing attaches to a marker. Deliberately not added to the regulatory set: only the Governor's office announcement could be read here, and the executed order itself is a PDF whose text this run could not extract. It is recorded here so a later run can promote it once the order is readable, which is how the Imperial Irrigation District tariff was handled on Sep 23 and promoted on Sep 24.

items.title: Pennsylvania PUC study puts PJM reliability risk at six times the standard
items.detail: The Commission released an independent analysis by Synapse Energy Economics on Sep 14, 2026. On PJM's current load forecast and with no further policy action it finds the regional grid fails PJM's reliability planning standard from 2027 through 2030, with modeled 2030 risk near six times that standard and, in a severe scenario combining higher demand with constrained new generation, more than 13 loss-of-load events a year from 2030. It attributes the demand growth largely to data center development, and notes projected new PJM data center demand for 2029 and 2030 alone exceeds the entire current annual electricity demand of Pennsylvania.
items.effect: No figure moved. This is a consultancy model of future reliability commissioned by a regulator, not a measured consumption series, so it fails Test 1 on the same ground as the EIA's Annual Energy Outlook projections and the Borderstep figure for Germany. It is recorded because it is exactly the kind of widely cited data center demand number a reader would expect this page to have accounted for, and the reason it is not used belongs in the ledger rather than only in a chat.

items.title: China's energy regulator gives a full-year figure for computing centers
items.detail: At the national AI-and-energy meeting on May 26, 2026, reported on the administration's own site on May 29, the National Energy Administration said China's computing centers used 170 billion kWh (170 TWh) of electricity in 2025, 1.6% of national consumption, and that 42 ten-thousand-accelerator clusters had been built. Its director, Wang Hongzhi, put computing-power electricity on course for 800 TWh by 2030, about 6% of national consumption, which is the same 2030 figure the China Electricity Council gave in September. This is the first full-year official Chinese value on the table, but it arrives under a third classification: computing centers is neither the narrow internet data services series (49.4 TWh, first half of 2026) nor the 260 TWh (2024) total this page uses.
items.effect: No figure moved. China stays on 260 TWh (2024), scope mismatch declared. Against the 31.9 GW of Chinese capacity the IEA counts, 170 TWh implies a load factor of 170/(31.9 x 8.76) = 0.61, inside the 0.3-0.85 band, where 260 TWh implies an impossible 0.93 - so on physical plausibility alone this figure would qualify, and it is the first Chinese number that does. It is held back for the reason the IEA's 485 TWh is held back: the whole capacity basis here is 2024, so pairing a 2025 energy figure with it would move China on a year mismatch rather than on evidence. Provenance is the second hold. This is a statement at a conference carried by a newspaper and republished by the administration, not a statistical release with a stated scope, so it still does not say whether telecom and 5G network rooms are counted. Recorded as rejected in policy.json, and it is the strongest candidate to date once a 2025 capacity basis exists or the series is published with a definition.

items.title: FERC accepts PJM's reliability backstop, then suspends it five months
items.detail: The Commission issued 196 FERC 61,245 (eLibrary accession 20260929-3099) accepting PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement in Docket ER26-3380, and at the same time opened a companion investigation, Docket EL26-108, into whether parts of it are just and reasonable. PJM filed the tariff on Jul 31, 2026 under the title 'Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy and Large Loads', asking for a Sep 29, 2026 effective date. Chairman Swett and Commissioners Rosner, See and LaCerte concurred with a separate statement. RTO Insider reported on Sep 30, 2026 that implementation is suspended for five months while the investigation runs.
items.effect: Nothing moves. The order procures generation against large load rather than measuring consumption, so no capacity or consumption figure on this page changes. Recorded in the regulatory set as evidence of data-center-driven generation, alongside the December 2025 co-location order and the June 2026 show cause orders it sits with.

items.title: Pennsylvania proposes cutting data centers first in a supply pinch
items.detail: At its Oct 1, 2026 public meeting the Pennsylvania PUC voted 4-0 to approve a Tentative Order, Docket M-2026-3064961, seeking comment on changes to how the state's electric distribution companies prepare for tight supply. New large loads that have not secured sufficient new capacity to cover their demand would be curtailed before other customers when PJM calls for load reductions under its proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service, and data centers could no longer be classified as critical load exempt from curtailment in pre-emergency or emergency events. Utilities would also have to keep a registry of large loads in their territory. Comments run 30 days from publication in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, with 15 days for replies, and a Final Order is anticipated at the Jan 28, 2027 meeting. A separate Technical Conference on allocating the costs of large computational loads is set for Nov 17, 2026.
items.effect: No figure moved. Curtailment priority and critical-load classification are not generation and not a measurement, so no capacity or consumption value on this page changes, and Pennsylvania has no mapped metro for anything to attach to. It is the item the Sep 22 entry said it was waiting for: that entry held the Pennsylvania set as it was until the tentative order arrived with a docket number, and it now has one. Added to the regulatory set as a fifth curtailment-or-cost instrument alongside Ohio, Oregon, Delaware and the Imperial Irrigation District. Recorded on the Commission's own release, which carries the docket, the vote and the four proposals; the executed order is now served on the docket as document 1952506 but its text could not be extracted here, so every statement rests on the release.

items.title: Texas has paused data center grid approvals since Aug 3
items.detail: Four directives from the Governor's office, read on his own releases rather than on an account of them: Jun 10, 2026, the PUCT to make data centers fully fund the electric infrastructure serving them; Aug 3, an audit of every data center in ERCOT's interconnection process, with no project advancing until it is finished; Sep 14, the TWDB to enforce water-use reporting under penalty; Sep 21, the TCEQ to issue no data center permits until the audit completes, with a compliance update due Oct 19, 2026. ERCOT is weighing about 474 GW of requests, roughly 90 percent of them data centers.
items.effect: No figure moved. Recorded in the regulatory set as txgov_audit. The mapped Dallas-Fort Worth inventory and the two mapped Texas campuses are already energized or already announced, so a pause on new approvals changes nothing here, and the 474 GW is an interconnection queue rather than capacity and is not used anywhere on this page. Found on a gap check rather than published this fortnight: the set held Texas SB6, the statute, but none of the executive directives that have since paused approvals under it.

items.title: North Carolina refuses a gas turbine over unverified data center load
items.detail: The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Sep 18, 2026 denied Duke Energy a certificate of public convenience and necessity for a sixth combustion turbine, 255 MW and about $584 million, at the Sherwood H. Smith Jr. Energy Complex in Richmond County. The commission held the application premature because staff has not yet vetted Duke's modeled load growth, about 70 percent of which it attributes to data centers, in the pending 2025 Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan case, and because Duke had not shown how much of the turbine's output would serve data centers or how those customers would pay for it. The vote was 3-1.
items.effect: No figure moved, and no North Carolina metro or campus is mapped on this page. Deliberately not added to the regulatory set this run, on sourcing: the order is linked from WUNC's report, but the Commission's document system sits behind a bot verification that was not cleared from here, so the order text was not read and every statement above rests on WUNC's account of it. Promote it to the regulatory set once the order itself can be retrieved and parsed. It would be the first entry in that set where data center load caused a generation permit to be refused rather than granted, which is why it is recorded now rather than left in a run summary.

items.title: Michigan approves 1,600 MW of new generation for a single data center
items.detail: The Michigan Public Service Commission on Oct 1, 2026 approved special contracts in Case No. U-22058 between DTE Electric and Google for a data center in Van Buren Township, Wayne County. Under a clean capacity accelerator agreement Google pays for DTE Electric to develop up to 1,600 MW of renewable energy and 480 MW of battery energy storage, developed, owned and operated by the utility, to help power the facility. The accompanying primary supply agreement runs 20 years, sets minimum billing demand at 80% against 50-65% in the general D11 large-load rate, and carries an early termination payment covering at least 15 years of minimum monthly charges. DTE Electric expects service to begin in December 2027 and maximum load by December 2028.
items.effect: No figure moved. Added to the regulatory set as mpsc_dte. Michigan has no mapped metro, and the Van Buren Township site is not in the campus layer, which comes from Epoch AI, so nothing on the page attaches to it; the 1,600 MW is generation rather than IT capacity and is counted nowhere here. Recorded because it is the most explicit instance in the set of generation being built because of data center load, with a megawatt figure and a named payer, where the rest of the set either requires a data center to bring its own generation or sets the terms for connecting to the grid. Found on a gap check rather than in the fortnight's news. Read on the Commission's own release; the order itself was not retrieved.

items.title: Texas regulators take up Xcel's large-load tariff, and Staff files comments
items.detail: Commission Staff filed comments on the application, the proposed notice and the proposed procedural schedule in Public Utility Commission of Texas Docket No. 60332, Southwestern Public Service Company's application for approval of large load customer tariff provisions, on Oct 9, 2026. Xcel Energy's Texas utility filed the application on Sep 25, 2026 and announced it on Sep 28. Under the proposed tariff, data centers and other large customers would carry the cost of the electric transmission, substations, interconnection upgrades and new generation needed to serve their projects, on commitments typically of 15 years or more backed by financial security, with minimum monthly payments while load ramps and termination charges if a customer leaves early. Texas Industrial Energy Consumers moved to intervene on Sep 29 and AXM on Oct 1, and the Commission's Order No. 1 of Oct 2 required the Staff comments.
items.effect: No figure moved. Added to the regulatory set as puct_sps_llt, which the set was missing entirely, and found on a gap check rather than in the fortnight's news. SPS serves the Texas Panhandle and South Plains, where this page maps no metro, so nothing on the map attaches to it; Dallas-Fort Worth, the only mapped Texas metro, is outside its territory, and no capacity figure is involved. Read off the PUCT docket sheet and Xcel's own announcement; the filed documents themselves could not be retrieved from this session.

items.title: Texas finds Xcel's large-load tariff application complete and sets a schedule
items.detail: The Public Utility Commission of Texas issued two orders in Docket 60332 on Oct 12, 2026. Order No. 2 granted a motion to intervene and addressed other procedural matters; Order No. 3 found Southwestern Public Service Company's large load customer tariff application administratively complete and its proposed notice sufficient, and entered a procedural schedule. The docket sheet carries 12 filings, against 10 on Oct 9, 2026, and was unchanged when re-read on Oct 14 and again on Oct 15, 2026.
items.effect: Nothing on the page moves. SPS serves the Texas Panhandle and South Plains, where this page maps no metro, and no capacity or consumption reading is involved; the existing Texas tariff entry is re-dated to Oct 12, 2026. The order documents themselves were not read, because the PUCT document server is unreachable from this session; the docket sheet is the source.
items.src: Public Utility Commission of Texas, Interchange docket sheet for Docket 60332

items.title: Oregon suspends Pacific Power's data center rate class until the end of 2026
items.detail: Docket UE 463 is PacifiCorp's Advice No. 25-015, Schedule 401, Service to New Large Energy Use Facilities, the Pacific Power counterpart to the Portland General Electric schedule the Commission approved in Order No. 26-239 on Jul 10, 2026. Chief Administrative Law Judge Alison Lackey issued Order No. 26-310 on Aug 31, 2026 suspending the tariff sheets' effective date until Dec 31, 2026, and the contested case is still in hearings: an intervention ruling on Oct 7, 2026, and Commission Staff's motion to admit pre-filed exhibits, with the declaration of Bret Stevens, on Oct 12, 2026.
items.effect: No figure moved. Hillsboro / Portland's 491 MW, from CBRE's North America Data Center Trends H1 2026, is unchanged, and a rate class is cost allocation rather than generation or measurement. The existing Oregon entry already said Pacific Power's schedule was pending with a decision expected before the end of 2026; that expectation now rests on a dated suspension order rather than on inference, and the entry is extended to say so. Read on the Commission's own eDockets docket sheet, which carries the order numbers, dispositions and filing dates. Press accounts describing Pacific Power's data center rules as already approved do not match the docket, and the docket is what this rests on; the orders themselves were not retrieved.
items.src: Oregon Public Utility Commission, eDockets docket sheet for Docket UE 463

items.title: China Electricity Council's annual power report carries no data center figure
items.detail: The China Electricity Council released its Annual Development Report on China's Power Industry 2026 at a press conference on Jul 14, 2026, announced Jul 15, its twenty-first consecutive annual edition and, on its own description, built on the power industry's statistical and survey data across thirteen areas including electricity consumption. The release reports that China's all-society electricity consumption passed 10 trillion kWh for the first time in 2025, up 5.0% year on year, and that installed generating capacity reached 3,896.64 GW at the end of 2025, up 16.2%. A scan of its text returns no figure for data centers, computing centers, intelligent computing or the internet data services industry.
items.effect: No figure moved. China stays on 260 TWh (2024) with the scope mismatch declared. The council is one of the bodies that could settle whether telecom and 5G network rooms are inside the Chinese definition, and its flagship annual statistical report is the likeliest place a defined series would appear, so the checked route belongs in the ledger rather than in a run summary. It is not a negative result about the report itself: only the release announcing it could be read, the report is a priced publication, and cec.org.cn has timed out from this session on three separate runs, so this rests on the council's release as republished by the CCPIT Electric Power Industry Committee, which names the council as its source.
items.src: China Electricity Council, release of Jul 15, 2026, via the CCPIT Electric Power Industry Committee

items.title: IEA's new data center report still gives no 2025 capacity figure
items.detail: The IEA published "Powering Artificial Intelligence: Strategies for integrating data centres into electricity systems" on Oct 14, 2026, a technology report prepared at the request of France's G7 Presidency that surveys policy, regulatory activity and corporate strategy in more than 34 policy jurisdictions covering about 90% of global data center capacity. It is now the newest IEA publication on the subject, ahead of the Apr 16, 2026 Key Questions on Energy and AI. Its executive summary carries hyperscaler capital expenditure above USD 700 billion in 2026, 45 TWh of power purchase agreements signed by operators in the first half of 2026 (up nearly 20% year on year), around 150 million tonnes of CO2 associated with data center electricity use, and 750 to 900 GW of additional grid hosting capacity that non-firm connections could unlock. A scan of its text returns no installed data center capacity figure for 2025, and no restatement of either the 415 TWh (2024) or the 485 TWh (2025) consumption reading.
items.effect: Nothing on the page moves, and the IEA hold stands. The 485 TWh (2025) figure is held back on vintage alone, waiting on an IEA 2025 installed-capacity basis to pair it with, so the world anchor stays at 415 TWh (2024) and kIea stays at 0.398. This was the likeliest candidate to end that wait and it does not: the GW figures it does carry are grid hosting headroom and rental cost per GW, neither of which is installed data center capacity. Read on the report's own overview and executive summary pages in the browser; the PDF was not retrieved.
items.src: IEA, Powering Artificial Intelligence, technology report published Oct 14, 2026

items.title: Texas ratepayer counsel intervenes in Xcel's large-load tariff docket
items.src: Public Utility Commission of Texas, Interchange docket sheet for Control Number 60332
items.detail: The Office of Public Utility Counsel, which represents Texas residential and small commercial consumers by statute, filed a motion to intervene in Public Utility Commission of Texas Docket No. 60332 on Oct 16, 2026, the Southwestern Public Service Company application for approval of large load customer tariff provisions. It is item 13 on the docket sheet, which stood at 12 filings from Oct 12, 2026 through re-reads on Oct 14 and Oct 15, 2026, and was still 13 when re-read on Oct 17, 2026. The intervenors now on the docket are Texas Industrial Energy Consumers, AXM and OPUC; the Commission found the application administratively complete and entered a procedural schedule in Orders No. 2 and No. 3 of Oct 12, 2026.
items.effect: No figure moved. A ratepayer advocate joining a contested tariff proceeding is a change in who is arguing, not a measurement: the docket decides who pays for generation built to serve large loads, and this page's capacity and consumption figures are untouched by it. SPS serves the Texas Panhandle and South Plains, where no metro is mapped, and Dallas-Fort Worth, the only mapped Texas metro, is outside its territory. Recorded because the existing regs entry claims a filing count and a last-read date, and both have now changed. Read on the Commission's own Interchange docket sheet; the filed motion itself was not retrieved, because the PUCT document server is unreachable from this session.
